itinerary.what: Born 10 November 1493 in a house near the bridge over the Sihl; spent his earliest childhood here until his mother's death.
itinerary.source: Britannica, 'Paracelsus'; Wikipedia, 'Paracelsus'; University of Zurich, paracelsus.uzh.ch (Life of Paracelsus)

itinerary.what: His father William, a physician, moved the family to Villach in Carinthia c.1502, where the young Paracelsus was schooled and exposed to mining and metallurgy.
Awarded a doctorate in medicine (and surgery) at the University of Ferrara around 1515-1516; earlier university attendance (Basel, Vienna) is reported but poorly documented.

itinerary.place: European wanderjahre (Italy, France, Low Countries, Scandinavia, Central/Eastern Europe)
itinerary.what: Years of itinerant travel, partly as an army surgeon, gathering empirical and folk medical knowledge; the precise routes and the more distant claimed destinations (Rhodes, Constantinople, Egypt) are largely uncorroborated.
itinerary.source: Wikipedia, 'Paracelsus'; Britannica, 'Paracelsus' (coordinates are nominal: Paris as a representative waypoint)

itinerary.what: Settled as a physician c.1524 after visiting his father at Villach; left amid the upheaval of the German Peasants' War (1525).
Acquired citizenship and joined the surgeons' guild in 1526 before being called onward to Basel.

After curing the printer Johann Froben he was appointed town physician and university lecturer (1527); lectured in German, and on 23 June 1527 publicly burned a copy of Avicenna's Canon, alienating the faculty and fleeing in 1528.
itinerary.source: Wikipedia, 'Paracelsus'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Paracelsus'; Hektoen International, 'The wayward Paracelsus'

itinerary.what: Stayed at Nuremberg in 1529 during his renewed years of wandering, attempting (with limited success) to publish.
Stayed at St. Gall in 1531, where the humanist physician and mayor Joachim von Watt (Vadian) gave him a cool reception; around this period he wrote the Opus Paramirum.
itinerary.source: University of Zurich, paracelsus.uzh.ch; 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Paracelsus'

itinerary.what: Published the Grosse Wundartzney (Great Surgery Book) at Augsburg in 1536, which revived his reputation late in life.
Returned to Salzburg under the protection of the prince-archbishop and died there on 24 September 1541, reportedly at the White Horse Inn.

relationships.note: Paracelsus's father, a physician at Villach, gave him his first instruction in medicine, botany, and mineralogy.

Traditionally named as a teacher, but Wikipedia notes no record of Trithemius at Einsiedeln nor of Paracelsus visiting Sponheim/Wuerzburg before Trithemius's death (1516); influence is more likely via his writings.

Paracelsus cured Froben's ailing leg in 1527; Froben's patronage opened Basel's humanist circle and led to his municipal/professorial appointment. Froben's death in October 1527 weakened his position.
Basel reformer who, with Wolfgang Capito, supported and sponsored Paracelsus's appointment as town physician in 1527.
The two exchanged correspondence on medical matters during Paracelsus's Basel period; Erasmus was a friend of Froben.
Humanist physician and mayor of St. Gallen who, per the UZH biography, 'gave him the cold shoulder' when Paracelsus stayed there c.1531; emblematic of the establishment hostility he faced.
On 23 June 1527 Paracelsus publicly burned a copy of Avicenna's Canon of Medicine in the Basel market square, a symbolic rejection of scholastic Galenic-Avicennan authority.

Paracelsus is the foundational figure of the iatrochemical tradition that Jan Baptist van Helmont developed and partly critiqued; later Paracelsians (e.g. Croll) and chymical physicians extend the lineage.
relationships.source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Paracelsus'; Bohrium, 'Paracelsus and the Rise of Iatrochemistry'

travel_note_html:
Theophrastus von Hohenheim, called Paracelsus, was born in 1493 at [LINK:einsiedeln] and grew up at Villach in Carinthia, where his physician father gave him his first training in medicine and mineralogy. After studies that culminated in a medical doctorate at [LINK:ferrara] around 1515-1516, he spent roughly seven years (c.1517-1524) as an itinerant army surgeon; the precise routes, and the more distant destinations later ascribed to him, are largely undocumented.

He settled briefly at [LINK:salzburg] around 1524 but left amid the Peasants' War, gained citizenship at [LINK:strasbourg] in 1526, and reached his greatest prominence at [LINK:basle], where curing the printer Johann Froben won him an appointment as town physician and lecturer in 1527. Lecturing provocatively in German and publicly burning a copy of [LINK:avicenna]'s Canon on 23 June 1527, he alienated the faculty and fled in 1528.

The remainder of his life was renewed wandering through [LINK:nuremberg] (1529), St. Gallen (around 1531, where Vadian rebuffed him), and Augsburg (1536), before he returned to Salzburg and died there in 1541. His chemical medicine became the seedbed of iatrochemistry, influencing [LINK:jan-van-helmont] and the later Paracelsian physicians.
sources: University of Zurich, 'The Life or Biography of Theophrastus Bombast of Hohenheim, called Paracelsus', paracelsus.uzh.ch/paracelsus-life.html
Bohrium, 'Paracelsus and the Rise of Iatrochemistry'
